feedback: When the child keeps offering examples: 'Those are all even, I agree — but could there be ANY two evens, somewhere, that don't work? How could you be sure without trying them all?'
When the child reaches for the pairs structure: affirm it — 'Now you've given a reason that covers every even number at once, not just the ones you tried.'
If the child says examples settle it: 'Examples show it works THIS time; let's find a reason it must work EVERY time.' — name that this move is a big step forward, not a failing.
For the disproof task: 'Just one case breaks it, doesn't it? One counter-example is enough to show an "always" statement is false.'
activities.intendedInsight: When there are endlessly many cases, as with even numbers, no pile of examples can establish a claim for every case, but a structural reason can — and a single counter-example is enough to disprove a general ('always') statement even though many examples cannot prove one.
learnerActions: State a general claim, e.g. 'adding two even numbers always gives an even number', and offer an example such as 4 + 6 = 10
Respond to a partner (an adult or a role-play) who cheerfully agrees each example is even but keeps asking: 'Can you give me another? And another?'
Face the key question: 'I believe every pair you've tried — but even numbers go on forever, so you could never check them all. How do you KNOW there isn't one pair that breaks it?'
Reach for a reason that covers all cases at once, e.g. 'every even number is made of pairs with none left over, so two of them still make complete pairs, so the total is even'
Then take a FALSE statement from the partner (e.g. 'adding two numbers always gives an even number') and topple it with a single counter-example such as 2 + 3 = 5
activities.title: Convince the friendly skeptic

feedback: If the child says only 'the answer's wrong': 'Point to the exact step — what should have happened in the tens column?'
When the child names the regrouping step: 'Yes — that's the broken link, and here's the place-value rule it breaks.'
Keep the focus on explaining the flaw; this is not an occasion to reteach addition from scratch.
activities.intendedInsight: Finding an error means naming the specific faulty step and the place-value rule it breaks, not merely observing that the answer looks different.
learnerActions: Examine a worked columnar addition that contains a deliberate error (e.g. incorrect regrouping between the ones and tens columns)
Locate the exact step that is wrong — not just notice the final answer differs from your own
Explain WHY it is wrong in terms of place value, e.g. 'the ten that should have been carried into the tens column was dropped'
Say what should have happened in that column to make it correct
activities.title: Spot and explain the faulty step
